correctness.rationale: With e_k the high/low squared spectral-energy ratio, direct substitution of r_k−r_(k−1)=−alpha_(k−1)Br_(k−1) in the RD quotient gives alpha_k=(a²e_(k−1)+b²)/(a³e_(k−1)+b³). Both mode filters are nonzero for positive finite e and e_(k+1)=e_k/(kappa⁴e_(k−1)²). The first residual Rayleigh step gives e_1=1/e_0. Thus phi=log(kappa²e) obeys phi_(k+1)=phi_k−2phi_(k−1), phi_0=2L+t, phi_1=2L−t. The roots (1±i sqrt(7))/2 give q=sqrt(2), cos(theta)=1/(2q), and phi_j=Cq^j cos(j theta−delta) with cosine coordinate 2L+t and sine coordinate (2L−3t)/sqrt(7). Their squared sum is 4L²+16(t+L/2)²/7, strictly positive, minimized at t=−L/2 (realizable by mixed data). The two negative log filter gains differ by uniformly bounded amounts from [phi_(k−1)]_+ and [−phi_(k−1)]_+, respectively, since log(1+kappa exp(phi))=[phi]_++O_kappa(1). Summing from k=1 to n−1 gives an O(n) log error including the fixed first step; after scaling, set m=n−j, so the first term of U is at m=2. Extending the series to infinity costs O(q^(−n)) and preserves uniform continuity. Opposite spectral phases give U and U shifted by π; comparing the Euclidean norm with the larger orthogonal component changes its log by at most log(sqrt(2)), hence the pointwise minimum H is correct. Four successive phases have gaps <π, so the finite part m=2..5 alone guarantees positive values of both positive-part sums at every phase, and compactness gives min H>0. The frozen irrational-rotation argument is also valid since 2cos(theta)=1/sqrt(2) cannot be an algebraic integer (its field norm is −1/2). This establishes the exact phase law, the double-log exponent and no mixed finite termination or geometric exception. On either nonzero pure mode the first step terminates. The conclusion is all mixed starts at fixed spectrum in exact arithmetic, not a one-step Q-rate or a uniform bound over coalescing eigenvalues.
